title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: enumerating every root-to-leaf path explicitly versus a direct recursive depth formula.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth, the number of nodes along the longest path from the root down to the farthest leaf node.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","root of a binary tree"],["Output","The maximum depth (longest root-to-leaf node count)"],["Goal","Compute depth recursively, combining each node's children's depths"],["Constraints","Up to 10^4 nodes"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Longest path from root to a leaf\"","A recursive post-order computation: a node's depth depends on its children's depths, computed first"]]}

blocks.text: The depth of a node is 1 plus the larger of its left and right subtree depths; an empty tree has depth 0. This recursive definition bottoms out at leaf nodes (depth 1, since both children are empty with depth 0).

blocks.title: Analogy: Measuring the Tallest Branch of a Tree
blocks.text: Picture measuring a tree's height by asking each branch how tall it is, then reporting one more than the tallest branch found, all the way down to individual twigs.
Maximum depth = 3 (root, then 9 or 20, then 15/7 under 20).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: An empty tree has depth 0.

Observation 2: A node's depth is 1 (itself) plus the LARGER of its two children's depths, since the longest path through this node follows whichever subtree is deeper.

Observation 3: Computing each child's depth recursively, bottom-up, naturally combines into the answer at the root.
This leads to a simple recursive function: depth(node) = 0 if node is null, else 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)).
Conceptually, enumerate every root-to-leaf path explicitly and track the longest one found.
Why the code is written this way

items: Recording every path length directly implements the definition.
This does unnecessary bookkeeping (storing every path length) when a direct recursive formula computes the same answer without an auxiliary list.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) nodes visited.
Space: O(n) for storing path lengths, plus recursion depth.
Limitation: the direct recursive formula avoids storing every path length, computing the answer with O(1) extra state per call.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Define depth(node) recursively: base case, an empty node has depth 0. Otherwise, recursively compute the left and right subtree depths, and return 1 plus the larger of the two. This directly computes the answer at the root without ever materializing individual paths.
Use a direct recursive post-order depth computation, combining each node's two children's depths.

Every node's depth is fully determined by its two children's depths, computed first (post-order), so the recursion correctly bubbles up the deepest path's length all the way to the root, without ever needing to track individual paths explicitly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n).
Space: O(h) recursion depth, where h is the tree's height (up to O(n) for a skewed tree).

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "find the longest root-to-leaf path", think: a direct post-order recursive depth combination.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches visit every node once, O(n); the direct recursive formula avoids the extra O(n) space for storing individual paths.

items: Pattern: post-order recursion, combining children's results into the parent's answer.
Core Idea: depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)), with depth(null) = 0.
Space: O(n) for the brute force's path storage, O(h) recursion depth for the direct formula.
Most Important Observation: a tree's depth is fully determined by combining its children's already-computed depths.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational, easy recursive tree problem.
One line memory trick: 1 plus the deeper child.
